traveler: Clotilde Sakharoff (Clotilde von Derp, born Clotilde von der Planitz)
title: The Hotel Union to the Protestant Cemetery: a dancer who invented her own line, and the man she danced it with
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Berlin, birth of Clotilde von der Planitz
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by both editions of her article and by the Neue Deutsche Biographie; English Wikipedia's article on her husband gives 1893 in body text, an unreconciled stray. No birth address is recorded, so the pin marks central Berlin only.
stops.campa: A daughter is born in Berlin to Major Hans Edler von der Planitz of the Prussian army and to Margarete von Muschwitz. The family is minor Vogtland nobility, the kind that supplies officers and gets its name into almanacs, and nothing in the household points toward a stage. The name she will carry for sixty years, Clotilde von Derp, does not exist yet, and no source explains where it comes from when it arrives. In the registers she is entered with four names: Clotilde Margarete Anna Edle von der Planitz.
suggested_refs: Frank-Manuel Peter's Neue Deutsche Biographie entry, which fixes the birth at 5 November 1892 in Berlin
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, entry by Frank-Manuel Peter

stops.name: Munich, the mother's music institute in Schwabing
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia attests the separation, the move and the institute and dates them to 1900 without month or day; the date defaults to 1 January. The pin marks Schwabing as a district, not an address.
stops.campa: The parents separate and the mother takes her children south to Munich, to Schwabing, where painters live cheaply and rents stay low. She opens a music institute for children and teaches in it. Within a decade the same quarter will produce the Blaue Reiter; for now it is the address of a separated woman making a living out of children's lessons. Clotilde grows up inside the sound of other people's scales. For a while she wants to be a violinist, and no source says what ends it.
suggested_refs: The Schwabing music institute for children run by Margarete von Muschwitz from 1900
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Clotilde von Derp' (the violinist ambition, which the German edition does not carry)

stops.name: Munich, modelling for the sculptor Wilhelm Krieger
stops.date_confidence: no source attaches any year to the modelling; 1905 is a placeholder inside her Munich girlhood. German Wikipedia names Wilhelm Krieger; the studio address is unknown, so the pin is the canonical Munich pin.
stops.campa: Before she is looked at on a stage she is looked at in studios. She models for painters and for the sculptor Wilhelm Krieger, holding a position by the hour while somebody else decides where the light falls. It is ordinary paid work in a city full of art students and short of money. She learns in it what an arm looks like from outside the body that owns it, which is the first technical knowledge she acquires and the only one nobody teaches her in a class. What she was paid, and for how long, is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Wilhelm Krieger's Munich studio, where she sat as a model before she danced

stops.name: Munich, ballet lessons at the Opera
stops.date_confidence: the teachers Julie Bergmann and Anna Ornelli are attested by English Wikipedia, which gives no year at all; 1908 is a placeholder. The source says Munich Opera, not court ballet school. Coordinates are the Nationaltheater's own, correcting a pin that sat some 160 m west.
stops.campa: Julie Bergmann and Anna Ornelli of the Munich Opera teach her ballet. In this city and this decade that means the five positions, the barre, and a repertory of historical costume. She keeps the discipline and refuses the repertory: what she starts making carries no story and wears no century of dress, and no company stands behind it. An officer's daughter who has modelled for sculptors is getting ready to walk on stage with nothing borrowed. Neither teacher leaves any account of the girl in the room, and no source gives the year she began.
suggested_refs: The ballet school of the Munich Opera under Julie Bergmann and Anna Ornelli

stops.name: Munich, the first public dances
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia dates her first public performances to 1909 without naming a venue or a month; English Wikipedia instead dates a professional debut to 25 April 1910. Both readings are carried, as separate stops, and are not reconciled.
stops.campa: She begins dancing in public in Munich, in rooms and halls that leave no programme behind. There is no company and no ballet master: one young woman moving to music in front of people who have come out for the evening. Isadora Duncan has crossed Germany in bare feet and a Greek tunic, and when the critics look for something to measure Clotilde against they reach for her, setting Clotilde on the far side, elegant and more modern. Word travels the way it travels in a quarter full of painters.
suggested_refs: Munich press notices of 1909-1910 on the first of the modern dancers

stops.name: Munich, the Hotel Union: debut as Clotilde von Derp
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English Wikipedia; the hotel's exact site is not given, so the coordinates are approximate central Munich. The Delius sentence is cited in German Wikipedia to Masken, 23 May 1910.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of April she gives her professional debut at the Hotel Union under a name that is not the one on her papers. Four weeks later the critic Rudolf von Delius prints the sentence that fixes her, and what he praises is an absence: no historical costume, nothing standing between the body and its own experience. Everything a dancer of 1910 is expected to bring on with her, she has left off. The Munich papers take up the word natural and do not put it down again. She is seventeen.
stops.quote: Diese Clothilde ist endlich einmal eine Tänzerin, die völlig eigenes Erleben formt, die sich von keinerlei historischem Kostüm gängeln lässt, die aus dem Reichtum ihres kleinen Herzens eine neue Welt entfaltet.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf von Delius, 'Clothilde von Derp,' Masken: Wochenschrift des Schauspielhauses Düsseldorf, vol. 5, 23 May 1910
suggested_refs: Rudolf von Delius in Masken, 23 May 1910, the earliest surviving critical account of her dancing
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Clotilde von Derp', quoting Delius

stops.name: Munich, Sumurun: Reinhardt's wordless pantomime
stops.date_confidence: the Neue Deutsche Biographie places her in Reinhardt's Sumurun from September 1910 in Munich; the day is unknown and defaults to the first. The 1912 dating in circulation is unsupported by that same source. English Wikipedia's claim that she held the title role conflicts with Wikipedia's own attribution of it to Grete Wiesenthal and to Camilla Eibenschütz.
stops.campa: Max Reinhardt is assembling a pantomime without words, an oriental tale carried entirely by gesture, music and light, and she is taken into it in September. Wordless theatre suits a dancer who has already thrown out the libretto. She is working inside the largest production machine in German-language theatre now, learning what a hundred bodies on a raked stage can do that one body in a hotel ballroom cannot. Which part does she dance? The record gives three names for the same role and does not choose between them.
suggested_refs: Max Reinhardt's Sumurun, Munich, from September 1910
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, entry by Frank-Manuel Peter

stops.name: London, Sumurun crosses the Channel
stops.date_confidence: the NDB places her greatest Sumurun successes in London in 1911, and Wikipedia's Grete Wiesenthal article independently dates the elaborate production's London run to 1911; no month, day or venue is named anywhere. The London Coliseum is the conventional attribution and stands in as an unsourced pin.
stops.campa: The pantomime travels to London and she travels with it. It is her first appearance before an audience that has never heard of Schwabing, and her largest success so far: a German expressionist experiment received in a West End house as spectacle. English notices dwell on her beauty and her grace, which is not what Delius had praised, and is what a foreign audience can see without being told anything first. She is eighteen and has never yet danced outside Munich under her own management.
suggested_refs: The London run of Reinhardt's Sumurun, 1911, venue undocumented in the reachable sources
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, entry by Frank-Manuel Peter

stops.name: Munich, the circle of the Blaue Reiter
stops.date_confidence: 1911 is attested as the founding year of the Blaue Reiter around Kandinsky, with Rilke and Yvan Goll named among her admirers. Her involvement with the Neue Künstlervereinigung München, founded in January 1909, is dated by German Wikipedia to the joint programmes after 1913 rather than to this year.
stops.campa: Kandinsky and the painters around him are pulling the object out of painting in the same square kilometre where she is pulling the story out of dance, and the premise under both is one premise: a form can be built without an inherited subject to hang it on. The Blaue Reiter is founded around Kandinsky this year and she moves in the circle. Rainer Maria Rilke admires her, and so does the poet Yvan Goll. Her own work with the Neue Künstlervereinigung München comes later, in the joint programmes after 1913.
suggested_refs: The Blaue Reiter almanac, Munich 1911-1912, and the Neue Künstlervereinigung München

stops.name: London, Dührkoop's portraits at the Royal Photographic Society
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia to 1913; no month, day or gallery address is given, so the date defaults to 1 January and the pin to central London.
stops.campa: Rudolf Dührkoop, the Hamburg portraitist, has photographed her, and his plates hang in London at the Royal Photographic Society. A dancer of 1913 leaves behind nothing but photographs and print; there is no film of her early solos and there never will be. What survives of the Munich years survives because a photographer with a reputation of his own thought her worth a session, and because a society in another country hung the result on a wall. She is twenty years old.
suggested_refs: Rudolf Dührkoop's portrait studies of Clotilde von Derp, exhibited London 1913

segments.name: The Painter Who Became a Dancer

stops.name: Mariupol, birth of Alexander Zuckermann
stops.date_confidence: the day is contested: English Wikipedia gives 13 May 1886, German Wikipedia 14 May Julian and 26 May 1886 Gregorian, and the two do not convert into one another. The English reading is used for the pin only; the contradiction stands unresolved.
stops.campa: In the Azov Sea port of Mariupol, Maria Polianskaja and Simon Zuckermann have a seventh son and name him Alexander. The town ships grain and coal and holds a mixed merchant population of Greeks and Jews; nothing in it suggests a dancer. He will change the name to Sakharoff, train as a painter, and stand on a Munich stage before he is twenty-five. Two calendars disagree by nearly two weeks about the day he is born, and nothing reachable reconciles them.
suggested_refs: The Zuckermann family of Mariupol, seven sons, of whom Alexander was the youngest

stops.name: Paris, the Académie Julian and the turn from the easel
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia dates the Paris period 1903-1905 and supplies the law study and the Sarah Bernhardt episode; English Wikipedia names the two academies without dates. The Académie Julian's principal address was the Passage des Panoramas, with rue du Dragon a branch atelier; the pin marks rue du Dragon.
stops.campa: He comes to Paris for law and stays for painting, working at the Académie des Beaux-Arts and the Académie Julian in years when a young Russian in Paris is expected to be at an easel. Then he watches Sarah Bernhardt act. What he sees is a single body organising a whole evening by itself, and it is enough to end the painting. Dancers his age have finished being trained. He leaves for Munich to begin, taking classical ballet and acrobatics from the first position.
suggested_refs: The Académie Julian and the Académie des Beaux-Arts, Paris, 1903-1905

stops.name: Munich, the Künstlervereinigung and the Jawlensky portrait
stops.date_confidence: both editions attest the 1909 membership of the Neue Künstlervereinigung München and the portraits by Jawlensky and Werefkin; no month or day is given. No source places the joining or the sittings at the Moderne Galerie Thannhauser, which merely hosted the society's exhibitions, so the pin is an unsourced stand-in. The Wikipedia article on the society does not name him.
stops.campa: He joins the Neue Künstlervereinigung München and works with Kandinsky and Thomas von Hartmann on the question of what a colour has to do with a sound. Alexej von Jawlensky paints him; Marianne von Werefkin paints him; both remark on how little the face declares a sex. His widow will sell the Jawlensky decades on, in the years when she is selling things off. It is the picture of him from before anyone had heard of him, and it is the one still reproduced.
suggested_refs: Jawlensky's 1909 portrait of Alexander Sakharoff, sold by Clotilde in her last years
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Neue Künstlervereinigung München' (checked and negative)

stops.name: Munich, the Tonhalle: Sacharoff dances alone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, verbatim, by German Wikipedia; the sentence is sometimes misattributed to the Dansmuseet Stockholm page, which is unreachable. The Tonhalle at Türkenstraße 5, the Kaim-Saal, was destroyed in 1944; coordinates are the recorded site of the building.
stops.campa: On the second of June he gives his own solo debut in the Tonhalle on Türkenstraße, in a piece built out of mythological motifs and Renaissance painting: a man dancing alone in front of a Munich concert audience. Thirty-eight days earlier, a mile away, Clotilde von Derp had made her debut at the Hotel Union. They have the same city, the same year, the same quarrel with ballet and the same handful of critics. They will not meet for another three years.
suggested_refs: The Kaim-Saal at Türkenstraße 5, Munich, destroyed 1944, site of Sacharoff's 1910 solo debut

stops.name: Munich, the Press Ball
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia places the meeting at a Munich press ball in 1913 and gives no month, day or venue; the date defaults to 1 January and the pin is approximate central Munich.
stops.campa: They meet at last at a press ball, in evening dress, among journalists. Two soloists who have each spent three years inventing a way to move without a company, and who each hold what the other lacks: he has the theory and the drawing hand, she has the line the notices cannot stop describing. The billing that will carry them for forty years begins as an arrangement of convenience. The first shared programmes fall in the same year, sometimes as a duo, sometimes as two soloists on one evening.
suggested_refs: The Munich press ball of 1913, at which von Derp and Sacharoff met

stops.name: Zurich, the neutral country
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia records only that the pair relocated to neutral Switzerland at the outbreak of war, naming no city and no month; Zurich is a stand-in pin and the date defaults to 1 January 1914.
stops.campa: The war shuts the German stages to a career built on touring and opens the Swiss ones. They cross into a country that is not fighting and go on working there, two foreigners with an act that needs no language. Five years of war and its aftermath pass. Which city takes them first is not written down in anything reachable; Zurich has the money, the exiles and the halls, and it is where Marianne von Werefkin, who painted him in Munich, has also ended up.
suggested_refs: The wartime Swiss exile of the German and Russian dance avant-garde, 1914-1919

stops.name: Berlin, the sculptor's letter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction rather than attestation: German Wikipedia carries the sentence and the year 1916 with no footnote of any kind, no publication, archive or letter collection, and no corroboration outside Wikipedia could be obtained. Neither the month nor the place of writing is recorded; Berlin is where Kolbe worked.
stops.campa: Georg Kolbe, who spends his working life deciding how a standing human figure should be arranged in bronze, writes to her in the middle of the war. He does not write about her to somebody else. He writes to her, in the second person, and the sentence is the most extravagant thing anyone puts into ink about her in her lifetime. She is dancing in a neutral country while he writes it from a Germany at war. Where the letter is now, and whether anyone alive has held it, the record does not say.
stops.quote: Zweifellos sind sie für mich die erste Tänzerin Deutschlands.
stops.quote_source: Georg Kolbe, in a letter to Clotilde von Derp, 1916, as reported without citation in German Wikipedia, 'Clotilde von Derp'
suggested_refs: Georg Kolbe's correspondence, in which the 1916 letter to Clotilde von Derp would sit if it survives
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Clotilde von Derp', quoting Kolbe without a footnote

stops.name: Zurich, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: 25 January 1919 is given by both editions of her article and supported by the NDB genealogy; German Wikipedia's own article on Alexander Sacharoff gives 25 July 1919 instead. The contradiction is internal to the same encyclopedia and is left open.
stops.campa: Clotilde von der Planitz and Alexander Sakharoff marry in Zurich on the twenty-fifth of January. The German record calls it a Zweckehe, a marriage of purpose, arranged to smooth an American tour that would rather book a married couple than two people travelling together. Whatever the reason written on the paper, neither of them will live with anyone else. Marianne von Werefkin signs as witness, the painter who had put his face on canvas ten years before in Munich. One article of the same encyclopedia gives the day as January, another as July.
suggested_refs: The Zurich marriage register, 25 January 1919, with Marianne von Werefkin as Trauzeugin

stops.name: New York, the Metropolitan Opera
stops.date_confidence: no source consulted gives any year for the Metropolitan Opera appearance, and the precise date of 17 February 1920 in circulation is unsupported by English or German Wikipedia or the NDB. The date here is a container only, placed after the marriage the tour reportedly required. Coordinates are the old Metropolitan Opera House at Broadway and 39th Street.
stops.campa: Edith Rockefeller pays for the American season and they appear at the Metropolitan Opera House on Thirty-ninth Street. It does not go well. What Munich had read as a new grammar of movement reads in New York as two Europeans in strange costumes doing something between ballet and mime, and the notices are thin. They keep the tour, lose the argument, and go back to Europe, where the audience already knows what it is looking at. No source records what they danced.
suggested_refs: The Metropolitan Opera performance database, the only place a firm date for this appearance might be recovered
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Clotilde von Derp', citing Toepfer, Empire of Ecstasy, 219-222

stops.name: Paris, the name on the bill
stops.date_confidence: the Neue Deutsche Biographie dates the Paris base to 1919; English Wikipedia gives no start year at all, saying only that they lived in Paris until the Second World War under the name Les Sakharoff. The 1922 sometimes quoted has no source. Coordinates are the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: They take Paris as a base and are billed there in French, Les Sakharoff, a plural that works as a trademark. Neither of them is French. From here the touring runs out and comes back: London, Monaco, the German cities, then further. He designs the costumes and much of the repertory; she dances the line the notices describe and he cannot. Their programmes are built of short solos and duets, each set to one named piece of music, and they will work out of this city for twenty years, between two wars.
suggested_refs: Programmes and posters billed as Les Sakharoff, Paris, 1919-1939
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, entry by Frank-Manuel Peter

stops.name: Paris, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
stops.date_confidence: the appearance at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées comes from the Dansmuseet Stockholm page 'The Sakharoffs', which now returns 404 and could not be read; treated as an unverified relay. No month or day.
stops.campa: They dance at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the concrete house on the avenue Montaigne that had opened eight years earlier with a riot over the Rite of Spring. The programme is theirs alone: no pit full of a new score, no company, no scandal, two people and a pianist and a series of pieces the length of a song. What the Sakharoffs sell is finish, each solo costumed to the second, down to the wig. Paris in 1921 is thick with dancers, and they are working the same season as all of them.
suggested_refs: The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées seasons of the early 1920s
sources: Dansmuseet Stockholm, 'The Sakharoffs' (page now HTTP 404, relayed only)

stops.name: Paris, the Barbier poster
stops.date_confidence: the 1921 poster by George Barbier is attested by English Wikipedia, quoting Lodder, Kokkori and Mileeva; no source places its making or printing in Paris, so the canonical Paris pin is a stand-in, and no month or day is given.
stops.campa: George Barbier draws them for a poster advertising the act, and the drawing states what a decade of criticism has been circling. It shows a pair whose sexes complete each other rather than oppose each other, joined in the dancing and not otherwise easy to tell apart. She wears trousers on stage; he wears skirts and a metal wig. Audiences who come for a scandal are handed a symmetry instead. The image is reproduced for the rest of their working life.
stops.quote: mutually complementary androgynous couple ... united in dance
stops.quote_source: Christina Lodder, Maria Kokkori and Maria Mileeva, Utopian Reality (Brill, 2013), 33-35, on the 1921 Barbier poster, as quoted in English Wikipedia
suggested_refs: George Barbier's 1921 poster for the Sakharoffs
sources: Lodder, Kokkori and Mileeva, Utopian Reality (Brill, 2013), 33-35, at second hand

stops.name: London, the Coliseum
stops.date_confidence: the Coliseum date comes from the Dansmuseet Stockholm page, now 404 and unreadable; German Wikipedia confirms London among their appearances without any year at all. Treated as an unverified relay, with the date a container.
stops.campa: They play the Coliseum, a variety house of two and a half thousand seats where a dance duet shares an evening with acrobats and a comic. It is the circuit that pays. Twice a day, six days a week, is how a variety house runs, and the act is cut to fit. None of what they wear is what a ballet company would put on a stage: the gold and silver wigs, the hats trimmed with wax fruit, the flowers sewn onto the costumes, all of it built to read from the back of a hall this size.
suggested_refs: London Coliseum bills of the early 1920s
sources: Dansmuseet Stockholm, 'The Sakharoffs' (page now HTTP 404, relayed only)
English Wikipedia, 'Clotilde von Derp' (costume description, editorial prose footnoted to Toepfer)

stops.name: Paris, Vuillermoz writes the method down
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia to 1933; no month or day is given, and the study itself was not located or read.
stops.campa: The critic and musicologist Émile Vuillermoz publishes a study of how they work with composers: which score gets chosen, how a piece of music is turned into a sequence of positions, what a dancer owes the man who wrote the notes. By 1933 the act is old enough to be documented rather than reviewed, and a musicologist has filed it under the history of music rather than the history of dance. They are in their forties. They have been on the same bill for twenty years.
suggested_refs: Émile Vuillermoz's 1933 study of the Sakharoffs and their composers, not located in this research

stops.name: Shanghai, the Far East tour
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia records only that the duo toured China and Japan and that an earlier tour succeeded well enough that they returned in 1934; it names no city. Shanghai comes from the Dansmuseet Stockholm page, now 404. Unverified relay, date a container.
stops.campa: The tour reaches Shanghai, a treaty port with European theatres, Russian émigrés and an audience that can be sold a Paris act. Two dancers whose entire method assumes a listener who already knows the music are performing it eight thousand kilometres from where that music was written. What is certain is that they went to China. Which pieces they brought, and into what houses, is not recorded in anything reachable, and the city survives on the itinerary as a name in a list.
suggested_refs: Shanghai's European theatre circuit of the 1930s
sources: Dansmuseet Stockholm, 'The Sakharoffs' (page now HTTP 404, relayed only)

stops.name: Tokyo, the return to Japan
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia attests that the earlier tour was so successful that they returned again in 1934, and names no city and no venue; the Tokyo Imperial Theatre is an unsourced stand-in pin and the date defaults to 1 January.
stops.campa: Japan takes them better than New York did. The first tour goes well enough that they cross the world a second time to repeat it, which in a touring career is the only review that counts. A country with its own long tradition of stylised male performance, of masks, of gesture inherited whole and taught without deviation, watches two Europeans do the deliberately unhistorical thing and buys tickets for it twice. No source names a theatre, a date or a programme.
suggested_refs: Japanese press coverage of the 1934 Sakharoff tour, not consulted in this research

stops.name: Montevideo, the Teatro Solís
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia says only that the couple visited both North and South America, with no year; Montevideo and the Teatro Solís come from the Dansmuseet Stockholm page, now 404. Unverified relay; the date is a container inside the touring decade.
stops.campa: The southern circuit runs down the Atlantic coast and sets them on the Río de la Plata. They come as a European novelty on a season's tour: billed, paid, shipped onward, one act among the companies working their way down the same coast. It is the first time either of them stands on the ground that will keep them through the next war. What they danced in Montevideo is not recorded, and neither is the month. They dance in the Teatro Solís, a nineteenth-century Italian house facing a river the colour of clay.
suggested_refs: Teatro Solís seasons of touring European companies, Montevideo, 1930s
sources: Dansmuseet Stockholm, 'The Sakharoffs' (page now HTTP 404, relayed only)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Teatro Colón
stops.date_confidence: the Teatro Colón appearance rests on the Dansmuseet Stockholm page, now 404; no other source names a Buenos Aires venue for the interwar tours. Unverified relay; coordinates are the canonical Teatro Colón pin and the date is a container inside the 1930s.
stops.campa: They dance at the Colón, the opera house Buenos Aires built to prove it was a capital, seven storeys of red plush under a dome. Every touring company of the century passes through it, and fifteen years from now this city will be where they live. Which evenings they filled, and what they danced on them, is not recorded in anything reachable. The Sakharoffs pass through as one more European act on a South American season, in silver wigs, before a house that has heard Caruso and will hear everybody else.
suggested_refs: Teatro Colón programme archives for the interwar touring seasons
sources: Dansmuseet Stockholm, 'The Sakharoffs' (page now HTTP 404, relayed only)

stops.name: Madrid, out of France
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia says they moved to Spain when France was invaded by Germany, naming no city and no date; 1940 is inferred from the invasion itself, and Madrid is an unsourced stand-in for a country the source names only as Spain.
stops.campa: The German army enters France and the Paris of Les Sakharoff ends after twenty years. They go to Spain, out of one dictatorship's war and into another dictatorship's peace, and wait. He was born a Russian Jew in Mariupol; she is a Prussian officer's daughter working under a stage name. Neither is a safe thing to be carrying across Europe in 1940, and Spain is the only land route left out of France. No source names the city they waited in, how long they waited, or how they got out.
suggested_refs: Spanish transit routes out of occupied France for stateless and Jewish performers, 1940

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the new base
stops.date_confidence: the dating is contradicted three ways and is not resolved: German Wikipedia dates the Buenos Aires period from 1938, English Wikipedia has them arriving after the 1940 invasion of France, and German Wikipedia's article on Alexander has him emigrating in 1941. All three agree the base lasts until 1949. Coordinates are the canonical Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: They settle in Buenos Aires, a city already full of Europeans who left in a hurry, and stay nine years. The touring stops and the teaching starts. Argentina in these years is where a great deal of European performance goes in order to keep working, and the Sakharoffs join it as instructors, carrying a repertoire built for halls in cities that are being bombed. Three sources give three different arrival years, from 1938 to 1941. All three end the period in 1949.
suggested_refs: The wartime European performing emigration to Buenos Aires, 1938-1949

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the separation
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia's article on Alexander Sacharoff says the couple separated and later reunited for artistic projects, without dating the separation; English Wikipedia mentions none. His 1948 return to Europe comes from the Dansmuseet Stockholm page, now 404. Both elements unverified.
stops.campa: At some point in the Argentine years they separate, and at some point they come back together for the work. Neither the parting nor the return is dated by anything reachable, and no source anywhere gives a reason for either. Thirty years of one billing and one costume trunk are not dissolved so much as suspended. The German edition alone carries the parting; the English mentions none at all. He goes ahead to Europe, in the account that survives. She stays in Buenos Aires and teaches.
suggested_refs: The undated separation and reunion of the Sakharoffs, recorded only in the German edition
sources: Dansmuseet Stockholm, 'The Sakharoffs' (page now HTTP 404, relayed only)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, danced music put into a book
stops.date_confidence: Reflexiones sobre la danza y la música was published in Buenos Aires by Emecé in 1949 (OCLC 637742007); no month or day is given. The book itself was not consulted, and both quoted sentences are English renderings taken from English Wikipedia.
stops.campa: In the last year of the Argentine exile he writes the method down and has it printed in Spanish in Buenos Aires. The claim it makes is the one that separates them from everybody else on the interwar circuit: not dance to music, not dance with music, but music performed by a body. The aim, he writes, was to carry the sense the music makes in sound over into the sense that movement makes. He names her in the sentence. She writes no book of her own, then or later.
stops.quote: Clotilde Sakharoff and I did not dance with music or accompanied by music: we danced music.
stops.quote_source: Alexander Sakharoff, Reflexiones sobre la danza y la música (Buenos Aires: Emecé, 1949), in the English rendering quoted by English Wikipedia
suggested_refs: Alexander Sakharoff, Reflexiones sobre la danza y la música, Emecé, Buenos Aires, 1949

stops.name: Rome, the last address
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia dates the move to Italy and the Chigi Saracini invitation to around 1950; the Dansmuseet Stockholm page gave 1952 for the Rome relocation but is now 404 and unreadable. Not reconciled, and no month or day is given.
stops.campa: Count Guido Chigi Saracini invites them to Italy and they take Rome, the fourth country they have lived in and the last. She is fifty-seven, he is sixty-four, and the touring career is finished apart from one Italian circuit. They keep an apartment and a studio, and the costumes, the designs and the photographs of forty years come with them and go into boxes. What remains after that is a city, a school and students. Neither of them will leave Italy again.

stops.name: Siena, the Accademia Musicale Chigiana
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia attests that Alexander taught at the Accademia Musicale Chigiana under Chigi Saracini and developed there his theory of danced music; no start year is given beyond the general placement around 1950, and no month or day.
stops.campa: At the Chigiana, a music academy inside a Sienese palace, he teaches dancers in an institution built for musicians. Students come for the summer courses. He tells them that the dancer's job is to make a composer's intentions visible, and then demonstrates it at sixty-four in a rehearsal room. The theory of danced music is worked out here, inside a building for musicians, and taught to dancers. Siena becomes their second address, the city the teaching happens in.
stops.quote: Our aim was to transpose the sense expressed by the music of the sounds, to the music of the movements.
stops.quote_source: Alexander Sakharoff, Reflexiones sobre la danza y la música (Buenos Aires: Emecé, 1949), in the English rendering quoted by English Wikipedia
suggested_refs: The dance courses of the Accademia Musicale Chigiana, Siena, under Guido Chigi Saracini

stops.name: Rome, a school of their own
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia records that they opened their own dance school in Rome, in the same run of sentences as the Chigi Saracini invitation and with no year attached. The 1956 sometimes given for the school is unsupported and conflicts with the source's own narrative order; 1950 is used as a container.
stops.campa: They open a school in Rome under their own name and teach in it together. A repertory built for two soloists is handed to people in their twenties who never saw the Hotel Union or the Coliseum. Nothing holds it but the bodies in the room: there is no notation and no film, and the steps go across by demonstration and by hand. Whatever of the Sakharoff manner outlasts them leaves the building inside a student. The students are Italian, and they are the last people to be shown the work by the two who made it.

stops.name: Rome, her last performance
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia dates her final stage performance to Rome in 1954, after which she only taught; English Wikipedia instead says the pair stopped dancing together in 1956, its infobox giving years active 1910-1956. Carried as two stops and not reconciled. No month or day.
stops.campa: She dances in public for the last time in Rome, forty-four years after the Hotel Union. There is no farewell season and no printed valediction: one account has her simply stopping, and teaching from then on. She is sixty-one. What she gives up is a thing she invented at seventeen with nobody to teach it to her, kept for four decades, and never wrote down. No source names the theatre, the programme, or who was in the hall. She goes on teaching in the school every week.

stops.name: Rome, the duo ends
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia states that von Derp and Sakharoff stopped dancing together in 1956 and gives years active 1910-1956; German Wikipedia's 1954 dating of her final performance is not reconciled with it. No month or day.
stops.campa: By this reckoning the duo ends in 1956, forty-three years after the press ball. Two dates stand in the record for the end, two years apart, and nothing reachable knows which evening was the last one. He is seventy, she is sixty-three. They go on living in Rome and teaching, and the billing that carried them across four continents is retired with no ceremony attached to it. Neither takes another partner and neither performs alone. The school stays open and the students keep coming.

segments.name: The Shared Grave and the Estate

stops.name: Siena, the death of Alexander Sakharoff
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by both English and German Wikipedia.
stops.campa: He dies in Siena, in the teaching city, at seventy-seven. Fifty-three years earlier he had walked onto the Tonhalle stage in Munich in a costume of his own design, a painter who had decided to be danced rather than to paint. She survives him by eleven years and keeps the school going. What she is left holding is a trunk trade: costumes, designs, photographs, and the papers of two careers that were never filmed. There is no company to inherit any of it.

stops.name: Rome, the Protestant Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: the burial at the Cimitero Acattolico is attested by English Wikipedia; the date of interment is not recorded, so the month of death is used and the day defaults to the first. Coordinates are the cemetery's own, correcting a pin that sat outside its wall toward Piramide.
stops.campa: He is buried against the Aurelian Wall in the Cimitero Acattolico, the ground Rome keeps for the non-Catholic dead. A Jewish boy out of Mariupol who became a French-billed dancer of German expressionist descent is put into Italian earth in the one cemetery in the city that does not require him to have been anything in particular. The plot will take a second occupant in eleven years. Cypresses, English poets: Keats lies a few rows off, and Shelley's ashes.

stops.name: Cambridge, the papers cross the ocean
stops.date_confidence: the Houghton Library holds Papers of Alexandre and Clotilde Sakharoff spanning 1922-1970; no accession date is given by any source consulted, so the stop takes the closing year of the span. Coordinates are the library's own.
stops.campa: Part of the written record ends up at Harvard: correspondence and papers running from 1922 to 1970, catalogued at the Houghton Library under both their names in the French spelling used on the bills. It is the half of an estate that does not photograph well and does not go into a display case. A researcher in Cambridge can read the letters of a partnership nobody in the building ever saw move. When the papers crossed the Atlantic, and by whose hand, no source says. The span closes in 1970, four years before she does.

stops.name: Stockholm, twenty-three costumes
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia states only that the Dansmuseet in Stockholm has held 23 Sakharoff costumes since 1973; it names no seller and no transaction, and the widely repeated claim that Clotilde sold them in the year before her death is an inference rather than a sourced fact. Coordinates are central Stockholm.
stops.campa: Twenty-three of the costumes enter the collection of the Dansmuseet in Stockholm, the dance museum Rolf de Maré founded out of the wreck of his own Ballets Suédois. It is the first large institutional holding of the two careers, and who handed the things over, or for how much, the record does not state. She is eighty and still in Rome. Metal wigs, embroidered coats, the wax fruit: objects built to be read from a third balcony, laid flat now in drawers.

stops.name: Rome, the death of Clotilde Sakharoff
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by both English and German Wikipedia; she was 81.
stops.campa: She dies in Rome on the eleventh of January, aged eighty-one. She had been Clotilde von der Planitz for eighteen years, Clotilde von Derp for nine, and one half of Les Sakharoff for fifty-five. There is no book by her, no film of her, no company carrying the name. What is left is what a photographer caught, what a critic wrote down in 1910, what her husband printed in Buenos Aires in 1949, and sixty-five costumes in boxes. She outlived nearly everybody who had seen her dance in Munich.
suggested_refs: Clotilde Sakharoff's death in Rome, 11 January 1974

stops.name: Rome, one grave for two
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia carries a photograph of the shared grave captioned Grab der Eheleute auf dem Nichtkatholischen (Protestantischen) Friedhof Rom; the date of burial is not recorded, so the day defaults to the first of the month of her death.
stops.campa: She is laid in the same grave as her husband, against the wall, under one stone that carries both names. The marriage had been recorded as a Zweckehe, an arrangement made in Zurich in 1919 to get a couple past an American booking office. It lasted forty-four years to his death and eleven more in her keeping of the school, and it ends in a single plot in a cemetery for foreigners, in a city neither of them was born anywhere near. Werefkin, who signed as witness in Zurich, had died in Ascona thirty-six years earlier.
suggested_refs: The shared Sakharoff grave at the Cimitero Acattolico, photographed for German Wikipedia

stops.name: Cologne, the archive buys the estate
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia to 1997: 65 costumes, hundreds of set and costume designs, and 500 photographs. The figure of about 300 designs sometimes quoted is over-precise and drops the set designs. Coordinates are the Deutsches Tanzarchiv at MediaPark 7; no month or day is given.
stops.campa: Twenty-three years after her death the German Dance Archive in Cologne buys what is left: sixty-five costumes, hundreds of set and costume designs, five hundred photographs. It is the largest single body of evidence that the act ever existed, and it sits four hundred kilometres north of the Schwabing where the work started. Everything in it is cloth or paper. Not one second of the dancing is in the purchase, because not one second of it was ever shot.
suggested_refs: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, MediaPark 7, holder of the Sakharoff estate since 1997

stops.name: Munich, Die Sacharoffs at the Villa Stuck
stops.date_confidence: the retrospective Die Sacharoffs: Zwei Tänzer aus dem Umkreis des Blauen Reiters ran in 2002-2003 at the German Dance Archive in Cologne and at the Museum Villa Stuck in Munich; the stop takes the opening year, and no month or day is given. Coordinates are the museum's own on the Prinzregentenstraße, correcting a pin that sat about a kilometre away.
stops.campa: The costumes come back to Munich and are hung in Franz von Stuck's villa on the Prinzregentenstraße, under a title that reads Two Dancers from the Circle of the Blue Rider. Cologne shows the exhibition first and Munich takes it after; the catalogue is edited by Frank-Manuel Peter and Rainer Stamm. Ninety-two years after the Hotel Union, the city that first argued about what she was gives her a room and a subtitle filing her with the painters. The wigs are still silver.
